This fundamental geometric fact serves as the basis for our proof that every assemblage of planar segments can be represented as a 2-dimensional spine.  This representation takes the form of a tree whose vertices correspond to subsets of the segments' endpoints and whose edges represent the simplest intersection points of 2-dimensional spines derived from these subsets. This new structure offers novel ways to think about the properties of arrangements and can be used to develop new algorithms for searching through arrangements in real 2-space. and MATLAB are widely used programming languages in various scientific fields, and their consistency across implementations is crucial for producing reliable numerical results.  Through the implementation of a simple numerical test, we examined the precision of basic operations in these languages, focusing on C++, Java, C#, Python, and MATLAB.  The test measured the accuracy of floating-point additions and multiplications at different precision levels, analyzing any discrepancies observed and drawing comparisons with the IEEE 754 floating-point standard.  To ensure unbiased results, we utilized three different compiler versions for each language, incorporating both 32-bit and 64-bit data types when applicable, and accounting for any operating system variations that might influence the outcomes.  The results showed that C++ and Java adhere strictly to the IEEE 754 standard, whereas C# deviates from the specification but produces reliable results nonetheless.  Python 3.9+ and MATLAB 2020b+ exhibit similar behavior, aligning with the binary64 format defined in the standard but failing to meet its requirements. We identified a magnetic flux tube that was highly twisted within a cavity filled with magnetic field lines of a lower density. This twisted tube was found near an area with reduced temperatures that is associated with the presence of a type of solar wave known as an inverse sense reversal wave. We perform a kinetic, particle-in-cell simulation of pair-driven relativistic shocks, focusing on the injection mechanism of particles and their resulting distributions.  Contrary to theoretical models, our findings indicate that electrons, rather than ions, are initially injected into the highest energy population within the shock precursor.  This distinct behavior is attributed to the important role that magnetic field instabilities play in front of relativistic shocks.  We observe that the Weibel instability acts quickly in the ion beam, generating a strong magnetic field that causes electron deflection and injection.  On the other hand, the beam-driven transverse instability affects the electron population more significantly, contributing to the formation of a second, more energetic electron population behind the shock.  These results offer a new perspective on the physics of collisionless shocks and the production of high-energy particles in relativistic jets.  Additionally, we contribute to our understanding of how particles are accelerated in shocks powered by the explosion of massive stars, as well as in those driven by the collision of relativistic jet components in active galactic nuclei.  We also explore the implications of our findings on the observation of Faculated Jets in active galactic nuclei.  Finally, we propose a new model for particle acceleration in relativistic jets, incorporating the insights gained from our simulations.  This model eliminates the need for the classical, shock-acceleration model, and we outline its potential applications in the study of jets in active galactic nuclei and the production of high-energy radiation in the explosion of massive stars.  We further conduct a survey of observed Faculated Jets in active galactic nuclei, analyzing their characteristics and searching for patterns that align with the new model.  This research offers a comprehensive understanding of the physics underlying the formation and behavior of faculated jets, as well as their observed properties.  We conclude that the simplest, most basic faculated jet structure can extend beyond $10^{17}$ electrons for a typical active galactic nucleus, making it detectable with current and future radio telescopes. Our solver is based on a preconditioned GMRES iteration, with a multigrid solver providing the preconditioning.  We use finite element methods to discretize the cardiac bidomain model, resulting in a linear system of approximately 10 million unknowns.  Our solver takes advantage of the sparse, structured nature of the underlying finite element matrices, using an implicitly assembled multigrid approach to speed up computation. This achievement is critical for large-scale numerical simulations of cardiac electrophysiology models, offering possibilities for the simulation of higher resolution models and the use of more complex models in clinical applications. This problem investigates the question of testing if a pair of integers is of the form k*B plus v times B for some positive integer k and an integer vector v, given that B is a given positive integer and the pair of integers is non-decreasing. This problem can be solved using a multi-dimensional integer range search on a data structure that includes all possible integer vectors of a given size n, with each point represented as a tuple of non-negative integers less than B, and has a time complexity of O(log(B) + log(B)^n) for each query, and a precomputation time complexity of O(B^2 * (B^2)^n) to construct the data structure initially. This solution utilizes a preconstructed data structure called the Modular Range Graph, which can be used to test pairs of integers of a given size n for a given positive integer B. We present three novel approaches to computing the source location, along with associated theoretical analyses, by drawing on concepts from geometry, algebraic topology, and graph theory.  We demonstrate that when the sensor locations form a general convex shape, a precise source location can be determined if at least four sensors provide partial information.  When the sensor locations form a simple convex polygon, we find that three sensors suffice.  When the sensor locations are curved but form a simple closed shape, we propose an approach using persistent homology that can handle a source location of any order, subject to certain conditions on the sensor network's geometry.  We also explore the minimum amount of information required for determining a source location in a network of sensor locations that form a simple closed shape, concluding that in the most general case, a source location of order three is necessary.  We further examine the scenario in which a source location of order two is feasible when sensor locations are linear, finding that an additional condition is necessary: the location of the source must split the line connecting two sensors into parts that are proportional to the sensors' distance from the source.  We apply these theories to a scenario in which sheep are being monitored using sheep trackers, demonstrating an effective source location method that requires minimal computational power, along with a proposal for optimizing the placement of trackers within a given area.  We conclude by presenting an approach for optimizing the placement of trackers within a given area in a pasture by drawing a pattern with fences that guides a sheep finder to the source of a sheep's signal with minimal search time, subject to certain conditions on the shape of the pasture and the placement of the trackers.   three young stellar objects: EHN12, EHN13, and EHN14, recently discovered 
  within the Perseus molecular cloud.  Using data from SPITZER and a dust model that 
  includes small grains, we examined how the observed emissions behave around these 
  objects.  For each source, we mapped the dust emission profiles and calculated

  that the profiles generally fit a power-law distribution, with most sources 
  exhibiting an inner slope of around 0.4 and an outer slope of approximately 
  1.  However, we observed variations in slope around each object, which we 
  attributed to specific factors influencing the dust disk emissions.  For 
  EHN14, we noticed a possible clearance in its disk's inner region, which may 
  indicate the object's mass is too low to maintain a full disk structure.  On the 
  other hand, we saw no evidence of a cavity in the disk of EHN12, despite its 
  relatively high velocity.  Additionally, we discovered a linear correlation 
  between the 24um dust emission peaks and the stellar masses of the objects, 
  which we took as an indicator of a reliable dust emission measurement method. 
  Overall, our research provides valuable information on the dust disk properties 
  surrounding these specific YSOs, which we hope will contribute to a more 
  comprehensive understanding of their evolution and development. While previous studies have failed to find a connection between this excess and the excess of positrons observed in low-energy gamma-ray spectra of binary systems consisting of a neutron star and a companion star, we have conducted a deeper analysis of this relationship.  Using data from T2K, SHINE, and a sample of 13 binary systems with low mass companions, we have explored the possibility that some of these systems could be responsible for generating neutrinos through the accumulation of low-energy neutrinos produced by supernovae that occurred in the past.  By analyzing the spectrum of neutrinos observed in T2K and SHINE and comparing it with the spectrum predicted by theoretical models of supernovae neutrinos, we have determined that, in general, binary systems with high mass companions and those with companions of low mass but high chemical composition are less likely to contribute significantly to the excess of neutrinos.  However, we have found that binary systems with companions of moderate mass but low chemical composition, such as those consisting of a neutron star and a companion of 0.5 solar mass, are more effective at generating neutrinos through the decay of accreted neutrinos rather than the degenerate neutrino component.  On the other hand, binary systems with companions of 1 solar mass or more, such as those consisting of a neutron star and a massive white dwarf, are more effective at producing neutrinos through the decay of degenerate neutrinos rather than the accreted neutrino component. Our system, 3D Generative Adversarial Autoencoders (3D-GAAE), employs two distinct neural networks that work in tandem to produce high-definition 3D models. Through theoretical modeling, we explored the formation of non-linear scattering resonances in polyatomic molecules upon hard x-ray irradiation.  Initial linear x-ray scattering spectra from theoretical frameworks like TDDFT and ADC(2) are insufficient for explaining the observed resonances in CO2 and N2O.  However, through the inclusion of non-resonant exchange-correlation effects, a resonance in N2O's spectrum aligns with an observed feature.  A more advanced, non-linear TDDFT approach that accounts for non-resonant x-ray induced polarization yields a resonance in CO2's spectrum comparable to an observed feature observed in micro-spectroscopy experiments conducted using the X-ray Laser Enhanced Spectroscopy (XLES) setup.  The results suggest that non-linear x-ray scattering processes could serve as a powerful tool for studying hard x-ray induced electronic transitions in molecular systems.  In N2O, a resonance that aligns with an observed feature in an experimental spectrum measured using an XLES setup can be attributed to a π*pi transition in a polyene-like morphology where N2+ and O delta+ share an electron.  In CO2, a resonance that aligns with an observed feature in an experimental spectrum measured using an XLES setup can be attributed to a π*pi transition in a ring-like morphology where CO2 delta+ shares three electrons. This method, called Informed Sampling, incorporates strategic randomness to enhance the effectiveness of existing training data. It works by intentionally degrading a subset of training data in innovative ways that mimic the characteristics of real-world data creation processes, such as image degradation found in image transformation techniques. In contrast to other data augmentation methods, Informed Sampling replicates the statistical processes that generate diverse data, allowing the network to learn meaningful inferences from partially completed data. This technique has several advantages over other data augmentation strategies, as it directly mirrors the data creation process, results in significantly less discrete, syntactic transformations, and effortlessly integrates with existing methods. In addition, it offers numerous possibilities for designing customized data creation processes based on specific applications and datasets.   remains a topic of debate. We aim to determine whether these sources emit X-rays through 
  a jet or a disk based on their behavior during outbursts observed in both X-ray and 
  optical wavelengths. Our research used data from the Swift and ASAS projects to analyze 
  the X-ray and optical peak times of outbursts exhibited by 12 BL Lac objects. We found 
  that the X-ray and optical components of these outbursts often peak at different times, 
  contradicting the standard external Comptonization model that links these components. 
  However, when we accounted for beaming effects observed in radio jets of these sources, 
  the peak times of the X-ray and optical components aligned properly. This alignment 
  suggests that these components originate from different regions of the jet, with the 
  X-ray component emerging from a more compact, faster-moving portion and the optical 
  component emerging from a slower-moving portion. This conclusion implies that powerful 
  extragalactic sources like BL Lac objects emit X-rays through a jetted geometry rather 
  than an accretion disk.     The observation that some BL Lac objects exhibit X-ray 
  flat spectra during certain outbursts is also explainable through this jetted model, 
  particularly when these sources experience a significant increase in their gamma-ray 
  emission during these outbursts. This research contributes to our understanding of the 
  physics governing powerful extragalactic sources like BL Lac objects and their place 
  within the broader context of active galactic nuclei.      One of the most notable 
  findings of this research is the discovery that the X-ray peak times of outbursts 
  exhibited by BL Lac objects correlate with the radio luminosity observed from these 
  sources at a separation of a few tens of parsecs from their central engines. This 
  correlation implies that the X-ray emission of these sources is driven by the expansion 
  and cooling of their jets rather than their connection to an accretion disk. This

One approach to understanding these patterns is by comparing them to random networks of a similar size and have similar characteristics, which allows for the assessment of their uniqueness.  One measure for accomplishing this goal is the average number of new connections found when scanning through all possible links between two specific components, which is sometimes referred to as the "first-contact sequence."  However, due to the massive sizes of information processing networks, calculating the first-contact sequence is highly challenging, which makes its analysis complex.  To mitigate this difficulty, we propose using an equivalent representation of the network, known as a matrix, which offers a novel perspective on the first-contact sequence by breaking it down into individual segments that correspond to specific edges.  This representation enables the identification of unique segments within the first-contact sequence of a network, which can be further analyzed for distinct patterns of connection.  In addition, this representation facilitates the calculation of various metrics, including the number of new connections found when moving from one state to another within the first-contact sequence, which can be done through linear time scanning of the network's matrix.  This approach is particularly useful for analyzing the structure of information processing networks and other complex systems with large, sparse connections, which often exhibit unique patterns of connection at specific levels of resolution.  This method can be applied to a wide range of systems, including biological networks, technological networks, and even the structure of documents in a database, which can be categorized based on keywords.  This approach offers various applications in understanding the organization of complex systems and the patterns of connection within them, which can be utilized in various fields of study.   accurate models: ResMap and ResPair.  However, prior studies have utilized a small set of
  conformational residues to train the models, potentially limiting their effectiveness when
  binding sites undergo conformational changes.  To address this limitation, we propose two
  new machine learning models: CAlphaResPair and ResPairPlus, building on the ResPair model by
  incorporating additional conformational information that should enhance its performance in
  situations where the binding site shape changes.  To evaluate these models, we conducted a
  comprehensive assessment on a large dataset of antibody binding sites, demonstrating that
  CAlphaResPair and ResPairPlus yield more accurate predictions than the original ResPair model
  for both binding site prediction and binding affinity prediction.  Furthermore, we observed
  that these models perform exceptionally well even when confronted with conformational changes
  that affect how antibodies bind to their targets.  To utilize these models effectively,
  we have also developed a straightforward protocol for predicting binding sites from unbound
  antibody structures that should be valuable for both research and industrial applications.

  antibody targets: PD-L1, a protein involved in immune suppression; SARS-CoV-2 spike protein,

  heart disease.  The results obtained using these models should be highly beneficial for both

We derive a concise closed-form expression for this disruption, which takes the form of a difference between two mutually informative amounts, analogous to the pattern observed in data compression theory for the disruption of conditional mutual information.  This expression's components can be further analyzed in specific scenarios where one or more sources have zero mean, which leads to conditions for the non-negative disruption of conditional mutual information.  We demonstrate that this disruption measure is applicable in three distinct communication scenarios: the broadcast channel, the multiple-access channel, and the general simultaneous channel model, which offers novel insights into each model's data compression limitations.  In the special case of the multiple-access channel, we derive an optimal joint source encoding scheme that surpasses the standard separate encoding approach by utilizing the newly obtained disruption measure.  This scheme's performance can be computed explicitly for a special scenario of the model where sources have zero mean, which results in almost identical performance to the ideal joint encoding scheme for the discrete model, demonstrating the effectiveness of this disruption measure in enhancing data compression efficiency in various scenarios.  This research contributes to our understanding of data compression limitations by providing precise closed-form expressions for the disruption of conditional mutual information in three distinct communication scenarios.  This research also offers novel insights into the disruption of conditional mutual information, which can be applied in other research areas such as information theory, machine learning, and statistics. They also noted that their technique could be applied to a class of linear time-safe petri nets that are recursively defined, incorporating a new characterization of safe nets in the process. We observe that their technique essentially computes the smallest fixed point of a mapping that defines the reachable states of a petri net, which bears a resemblance to fixed-point mu-calculus. We also note that our description includes an error estimate that was not provided in their original paper. Building on our reinterpretation, we offer an enhancement of their approach by replacing the saturation over places with a more efficient computation over transitions, which we term transition saturation. We demonstrate that their original characterization still holds when using transition saturation, additionally contributing two new characterizations of safe nets along with their recursive definitions. We apply the transition saturation approach to validate reachability properties of linear time-safe petri nets for the first time, which takes advantage of a more efficient computation at no additional cost. We further demonstrate that their original description still holds when replacing place saturation with transition saturation in three other cases of safe petri nets. We propose a unified framework of transition saturation over various classes of safe petri nets, which includes linear time-safe petri nets, safe petri nets with a bounded number of marked transitions, safe petri nets that are recursively defined, safe petri nets with a finite number of safe suffixes, safe petri nets with a finite number of safe prefixes, safe petri nets that are recognizable, safe petri nets with a decidable reachability question, and safe petri nets with a finite number of safe patterns. We demonstrate that all these classes share a common property where the reachable transitions of a petri net can be represented through a finite automaton, which serves as a necessary and sufficient condition. We offer an alternative characterization of safe petri nets through a disjunctive definition over transition saturation for the first time. We apply the unified framework to validate reachability properties of a chemical reaction network with a bounded number of molecule species for the first time, which takes advantage of a more efficient computation at no additional cost. We further apply the framework to validate reachability properties of a chemical reaction network with an unbounded number of molecule species whose reachable configurations can be represented through a finite automaton for the first time.   Compared to reference-based IQA methods, which require a high-quality reference image for evaluation, point-wise IQA methods are more desirable due to their ability to judge image quality without a reference image.
  With the rising use of deep learning in various applications, a growing number of point-wise IQA methods have employed a dataset-driven approach, leading to significant performance gains.
  However, Repetitive Information with Feedback (RIFE) distortion, which occurs when reconstructing a high-quality image from a compressed or distorted one, is notoriously difficult to tackle due to its complex, dynamic nature.
  In an attempt to address this challenge, this paper proposes a new point-wise IQA method called Attention-Aware Residual Learning with RIFE, which utilizes three components: a quality estimator network, an attention-aware residual learning module, and a quality-aware loss function. 
  By leveraging the true RIFE distortion process and providing true RIFE distortion data, this method achieves outstanding performance over existing point-wise IQA methods, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and MOS scores of 13.3%, 8.5%, and 23.8% respectively. 
  This method also offers impressive performance when evaluated using real-world image compression and real-world blended RIFE distortion data. 
  Furthermore, this research presents extensive experimental results to analyze the effectiveness of the proposed quality-aware loss function and the importance of true RIFE distortion data. 
  This research demonstrates that true RIFE distortion data is essential for point-wise IQA method performance, surpassing performance achieved with reconstructed RIFE distortion data by 130.5% in SSIM score and 10.3% in PSNR score.

As a groundbreaking application of this capability, we have employed an infrared laser beam to arrange and reshape another infrared laser beam's phase within a quantum gas. This phase-engineered beam then acts as a 2D grating that diffracts other nearby atoms, allowing for the control of their direction and scattering patterns. This technique's effectiveness was demonstrated by observing the behavior of $^{87}$Rb atoms after the phase-engineered beam was moved and modified. This phase-engineered approach offers a versatile method for creating 2D optical lattices and bragg gratings within quantum gases, potentially expanding their uses in research on many-body systems and the study of lattices themselves. Furthermore, it provides a practical means of creating Bragg resonances in 2D optical lattices by shutting off the driving laser that produces the grating structure, allowing researchers to observe Bragg oscillations in gases of $^{87}$Rb atoms for the first time. This research contributes to the development of sophisticated control methods over quantum gases, which can be applied in various areas, including the study of many-body systems, the behavior of magnetic fluids, and the creation of persistent currents in closed Bose systems.  In an extension of this study, the phase-engineered Bragg grating technique was utilized to observe Bragg oscillations in gases of $^{87}$Rb atoms for the first time. By varying the period of the grating structure, researchers were able to control the Bragg oscillation frequency, which correlated with the velocity of atoms after they scattered on the grating. We implement the Kowalewski polyonomials through the Lucas theorem, enabling precise computation of binomial coefficients and resulting in significant reduction of noise in the initial conditions.  We also develop a consensus on appropriate variables for the problem at hand, choosing rapidity as a key coordinate due to the problem's boost invariance.  With these adjustments, we are able to directly compare numerical constructions of initial conditions through the Bragg scale expansion and the Kowalewski polyonomials for the first time.  We observe that the Bragg scale expansion fails to accurately represent noise correlations, whereas the Kowalewski polyonomials succeed by several orders of magnitude.  We attribute this success to the Kowalewski polyonomials' capability to capture dissipative fluidic effects through a more precise representation of noise correlations, leading to improved performance in hydrodynamic simulations.  We demonstrate this by simulating a 2000 times compressed and 1000 times sheared gluon field scenario, where a $10^{-5}$ initial energy density is achieved through a $10^{-8}$ initial temperature, resulting in a 10 times greater simulation time using the Kowalewski polyonomials over the Bragg scale expansion.  We additionally provide Mathematica code for implementing the Kowalewski polyonomials.  We anticipate the Kowalewski polyonomials to be universally useful for noise correlation initial conditions in hydrodynamic simulations.  We further explore the Kowalewski polyonomials' applicability to 3rd-order dissipative fluid models and noise correlation initial conditions through a case study of a 2-component system, demonstrating its viability by precisely computing a 3rd-order noise correlation through the Lucas theorem for the first time.  We conclude that the Kowalewski polyonomials offer noise reduction advantages over Bragg scale expansions in initial condition constructions for both 2nd and 3rd-order dissipative fluid models.  We observe that Bragg scale expansions fail to accurately represent noise correlations through Bragg-Bloch oscillations, whereas the Kowalewski polyonomials succeed by several orders of magnitude in both cases.  We attribute this success to the Kowalewski polyonomials' capability to capture dissipative fluidic effects through a more precise representation of noise correlations.

isy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) machines, are significantly constrained by errors that occur during quantum operations and the limited number of qubits available.  As a result, NISQ computers are not yet capable of efficiently solving complex quantum problems through straightforward simulation, leading to a growing interest in implementing complex quantum techniques within NISQ machines themselves.  One potential approach is to utilize NISQ computers to perform quantum metrology, a technique that measures the accuracy with which specific parameters, such as phase angles, can be determined.  In an effort to explore the potential of NISQ computers in performing quantum metrology, researchers have been investigating different implementations of the technique.  One specific variation under scrutiny is the multi-parameter quantum metrology technique (MP-TOMA), which aims to accurately measure multiple parameter properties of a quantum system.  In a recent study, researchers proposed an all-encompassing framework for implementing MP-TOMA using NISQ machines.  This framework consists of three distinct phases: an initial phase where the system's parameters influence a quantum system's properties; a measurement phase where a NISQ computer performs quantum metrology on the system's properties; and an information processing phase where the computer processes the measured data to determine the system's parameters.  Utilizing this framework, researchers can effectively implement MP-TOMA in a variety of quantum systems, including optical systems and ultracold atomic systems, and can explore different implementation scenarios to achieve the most precise measurement results possible.  By exploring these scenarios, researchers may be able to identify new systems suitable for MP-TOMA and develop more efficient implementation methods.  Furthermore, the study finds that, in certain situations, NISQ computers may not be capable of accurately implementing MP-TOMA through straightforward implementation of the technique.  In these cases, researchers can use the framework to identify ways to optimize the technique within the limitations of the NISQ machine.  By doing so, researchers can maximize the precision with which NISQ computers can perform quantum metrology on complex quantum systems.  In addition, the study observes that the framework can be applied to various systems and scenarios, making it a valuable tool for the quantum metrology community.  By contributing to our understanding of how to implement MP-TOMA in NISQ machines, the research has the potential to enhance the accuracy with which NISQ computers can perform quantum metrology on complex quantum systems.  This research is relevant to a variety of areas, including the characterization of quantum systems,

Our research introduces a novel, compact way to represent neural network architectures, using a recursive autoencoder, which we call RecNet. The process by which an exciton breaks apart into an electron and a hole is referred to as exciton dissociation. This process is critical for using 2D materials in photovoltaic devices that harness sunlight to generate electricity. For an exciton to dissociate, the electron and hole need to become separated, which requires an external electric field to drive their division. In materials with high exciton binding energies, an external electric field is insufficient to split an exciton, making it challenging for the exciton to dissociate. TMD materials have high exciton binding energies, making exciton dissociation difficult without a strong external electric field. However, TMD materials paired with a polymer like P3HT can effectively dissociate excitons due to the material's unique electronic properties that enable the separation of electrons and holes. The polymer's π-orbitals overlap more easily than TMD materials' orbital, making it more susceptible to an external electric field that can drive the separation of an exciton into an electron and a hole. Once an exciton dissociates, the electron and hole need to be collected by electrodes to generate a photocurrent. The polymer's conductive nature allows it to collect electrons while the TMD material collects holes. The difference in charge carrier behavior between the TMD material and the polymer is a key factor in exciton dissociation. The energy level alignment of TMD materials and polymers is another critical aspect that influences exciton dissociation. For an exciton to dissociate, the energy level of the TMD material needs to be higher than that of the polymer to ensure that electrons move towards the polymer and holes towards the TMD material. The performance of hybrid TMD-polymer devices in converting sunlight into electricity is measured by their photocurrent density and onset voltage. The device's ability to generate a photocurrent indicates the successful dissociation of excitons, while the onset voltage determines the minimum voltage required for exciton dissociation to occur. Hybrid TMD-polymer devices with better performance have higher photocurrent densities and lower onset voltages. The performance of hybrid TMD-polymer devices can be improved by optimizing the material's properties and the device's structure. For example, using a TMD material with a lower binding energy or increasing the TMD material's thickness can enhance exciton dissociation. Additionally, varying the polymer's composition or using a different polymer altogether can improve the device's performance

One proposed approach involves using rewriting systems, specifically targeted rewriting strategies, to resolve equivalence.  We have conducted initial experiments using Kowalczyk's strategy and Kowalczyk-Reynolds strategy on a large dataset of preprocessed problems.  The results demonstrate that applying rewriting repeatedly until no further changes occur resolves equivalence in the majority of cases.  However, we also found instances where this approach fails. One example problem, (p OR not p) implications (q OR not q), resolves equivalence using Kowalczyk's strategy but not Kowalczyk-Reynolds'. A similar pattern emerges when applying Kowalczyk-Reynolds' strategy to a problem's variant, (p OR not p) implications (q OR not q) AND (r OR not r).  This pattern enables us to extend our initial results, offering a new method for resolving equivalence in certain binary connectives' compositions.  We aim to build on these findings to develop a unified framework for resolving semantic equivalence in first-order logic. Our primary goal was to compare the majority and proportional representation voting systems by analyzing their stability levels within this specific model.  Our initial findings revealed that the majority voting system is more prone to instability when altering the issues at hand, whereas the proportional representation system is more susceptible to instability when shifting the priority of one issue over the other.  To further explore these characteristics, we developed a graphical representation of possible scenario combinations for each system.  Our results demonstrate that the majority voting system becomes unstable if both issues are valued equally or if one issue is highly valued over the other, whereas the proportional representation system falls apart if one issue is significantly more valuable than the other, regardless of its absolute value.  We also observed that both systems yield the same stable outcomes when both issues are valued equally.  To expand our understanding, we introduced a metric to evaluate the impact of issue importance on stability levels.  Our findings indicate that the majority voting system is more resilient to slight changes in issue importance, whereas the proportional representation system withstands more significant changes before deteriorating.  To conclude, we analyzed how varying the weight of issue importance affects the stability of each system through a series of numerical experiments.  Our results suggest that the majority voting system performs better in scenarios with equally valued issues and deteriorates more slowly in scenarios with disproportionately valued issues, whereas the proportional representation system excels in scenarios with significantly valued issues and deteriorates more rapidly in scenarios with lightly valued issues.  Finally, we examined the behavioral differences of two groups of agents with distinct cultural backgrounds that make decisions on issues with varying levels of importance.  Our findings indicate that the majority voting system yields more culturally sensitive outcomes when issues are of equal importance, whereas the proportional representation system produces more culturally sensitive outcomes when more culturally significant issues are considered more valuable.  Our research contributes to our understanding of how different voting systems accommodate cultural differences and variation in issue importance within a specific model.  Our results are not theoretically generalized to accommodate other models of voting.  Our research advises policymakers on the suitability of voting systems for resolving conflicts within and between culturally diverse groups on issues of differing importance.  Our research offers practical insights for policymakers, whereas our methodology contributes to the theoretical foundation of cooperative game theory.  Our research has real-world applications in politics, economics, and social sciences.  Our research offers an alternative approach to analyzing cooperative game theory through the study of voting models.   their estimation from noisy data is a well-studied problem, with existing methods like MUSIC
  and ESPRIT yielding precise results for limited data. As more data becomes available, though,
  these methods cease to provide accurate results due to their fundamental reliance on matrix
  inversion.  In contrast, we propose a novel approach to estimating Fourier series coefficients
  from noisy data, one that leverages the geometric properties of sinusoidal signals instead
  of matrix theory.  By doing so, this new method can deliver accurate results even with an
  excessively high data dimension, making it particularly suitable for applications involving
  wideband signals.  Furthermore, this method's resilience to noise means that quality standards
  for data typically require reevaluation, allowing for more flexible implementation options.

  utilizes the angle between signal subspaces rather than matrix inversion, along with an overall
  framework for analyzing this approach.  Building on this framework, we derive a specific formula
  for estimating Fourier series coefficients from noisy data, plus an analytical expression for
  its variance.  With this variance expression in hand, we are able to investigate the fundamental
  limitations of this approach by analyzing conditions for accurate results and power scalability
  characteristics.  Expanding on these characteristics, we explore applications of the method

  the theoretical findings through numerical simulations, providing additional context with a real
 -world example involving a wideband signal reception system.  Throughout the paper, we utilize a
  fundamental signal processing concept - Fourier series decomposition - rather than a derived

By applying a joint layer to the typical fine-tuning process, our approach dubbed as TILDE, enables the model to generate descriptive words for unfamiliar contexts, thereby producing beneficial information for low-quality or outside-the-training-data situations.  Extensive experiments on three low-resource languages (Inuktitut, a polysynthetic language, and Amharic and Wolof, both agglutinating languages) demonstrate the effectiveness of TILDE in improving the accuracy of language modeling and achieving impressive results in low-resource classification tasks.  The code for our method has been made publicly available.  Overall, our research contributes valuable insights into effectively utilizing pre-trained language models on limited datasets and explores their applicability on diverse low-resource languages.  Additionally, our findings suggest that pre-trained language models with a high number of parameters exhibit better performance in generating descriptive words, although this is dependent on the specific characteristics of the language at hand.  Furthermore, our research indicates that pre-trained language models with a high number of parameters may not always yield the best outcomes due to increased computational costs and are more susceptible to bias.  Nevertheless, our results demonstrate that pre-trained language models with a high number of parameters have a higher potential for descriptive word generation, which could be exploited in various situations.  This research also offers a comprehensive analysis of how pre-trained language models with a high number of parameters generate descriptive words and provides a feasible method for removing biased information.   inference, particularly renowned for their effectiveness in estimating posterior
  distributions. However, MCMC methods require significant computational resources,
  which can be a major constraint, especially when working with complex models and
  large datasets. To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive MCMC simulation
  scheme that prioritizes efficient exploration of the posterior distribution in
  the initial stages of the simulation, with the aim of obtaining well-mixed samples
  quickly. These samples can then be used to evaluate the acceptance probability
  for a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, which accepts or rejects proposed parameter
  moves based on the ratio of the targeted posterior distribution to the sample
  density. The key feature of this scheme is the use of a self-teaching state
  machine that learns how to generate proposals on the fly, allowing for true
  posterior exploration and simulation for the first time in an unexplored region
  of the parameter space. The adaptive MCMC scheme offers several benefits,
  including the capability to utilize prior knowledge of the posterior distribution
  if available, the option to employ different state machines for various model
  parameters, and the ability to implement sophisticated proposal distributions
  through complex state machines. What's more, the scheme is fully compatible with
  block Metropolis-Hastings algorithms and MCMC diagonal or Cholesky matrix
  variance reduction techniques. We have implemented the adaptive MCMC scheme in an
  available software package called "adaptiveMCMC" and made it publicly
  accessible on GitHub. We have also demonstrated the effectiveness of the
  adaptive MCMC scheme through a range of realistic simulations, including one
  large-scale simulation involving over 200,000 parameters. The results indicate
  that the scheme delivers well-mixed samples quickly, which can be utilized to
  evaluate the posterior distribution accurately. We have also applied the adaptive
  MCMC scheme to three real-world datasets, consisting of 50, 500, and 20,000
  parameters respectively, which yielded posterior samples of high quality for
  all cases. The software package "adaptiveMCMC" is available on GitHub at
  <https://github.com/alanbakker/adaptiveMCMC>.  Registered Replication Reports

One area where large-sized optimization problems persist is network science, specifically within the context of the minimum Steiner tree problem, a fundamental issue with far-reaching implications for various communication systems, particularly wireless networks.  The minimum Steiner tree problem involves connecting a group of isolated nodes through the minimum number of edges possible in a graph, with the added condition that certain nodes are already connected and can serve as intermediaries or "helpers" to facilitate the connection.  For situations where precise solutions are not feasible to compute exactly, approximate methods can provide viable alternatives, with metaheuristics and local search techniques being popular options due to their simplicity and effectiveness.  However, these methods have limitations, as they rely on random starting points and may get stuck in local optima, leading to inconsistent results when applied to different instances of the same problem.  To address these drawbacks, we propose an innovative local search framework called "Smart" for solving the minimum Steiner tree problem, featuring a sophisticated initialization strategy to counteract the issue of local optima and an adjustable "smartness" parameter to balance exploration and exploitation.  Our smart local search approach differs significantly from conventional local search methods by initiating solving processes from high-quality feasible solutions, obtained through a polynomial-time algorithm known as the "branch-and-bound" algorithm, rather than random starting points.  Our research includes comprehensive performance testing of the smart local search framework on large-sized instances of the minimum Steiner tree problem in real-world scenarios from wireless communication systems, along with theoretical analyses to guarantee the algorithm's quality and efficiency. As the point cloud's motion is not without limitation, areas of $B$ not visible to the point cloud cannot be directly included in the cloud.  We explore the problem of computing a shape that represents the best fit for $K$ within the boundaries of $B$, which we define as the "nicest" version of the problem due to the point cloud's limitations.  We introduce an approach to approximate the shape of $K$ as a collection of polygonal regions if the boundary of $B$ is polygonal, which involves reconstructing the boundary of $B$ or using an existing method if it is not.  If the boundary of $B$ is a smooth curve, we propose an alternative approach that approximates the shape of $K$ using a mesh.  In both cases, we provide algorithms to compute the shape of $K$ along with estimates of their complexity.  If the boundary of $B$ is a polygon with $n$ vertices, both algorithms take time $O(n\log n)$ to complete if the point cloud consists of $m$ points and the shape of $K$ consists of $T$ regions.  If the boundary of $B$ can be represented using a mesh with $T'$ triangles, the second algorithm takes time $O(T'\log T')$ to complete.  If the boundary of $B$ has a convex polygonal part with $s$ vertices, the first algorithm takes time $O(s^2\log s)$ to complete if the shape of $K$ consists of $T$ regions.  The overall complexity of both algorithms scales linearly with respect to the total number of points in the point cloud.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a set of experimental results on real-world data sets. D grid layouts of wireless sensor networks (WSNs) through a novel problem called Maximum Weighted Inside Vertex Deck (MWIVD). The goal of MWIVD is to identify the minimum number of sensors required to decompose a portion of the network by removing the smallest number of sensors while maximizing the coverage of remaining sensors. This problem's significance lies in its potential to enhance network durability and overall performance. To solve MWIVD, we propose an algorithm that consists of two main parts: identifying the Maximum Inside Vertex Pack (MIVP) and determining the Maximum Weighted Edge Cover (MWEC). We utilize a combination of graph theoretical concepts, specifically inside vertex packs, edge covers, and matching to solve this problem. We also provide a polynomial-time solution for MWIVD by utilizing the following approaches: finding MIVP and MWEC through a brute-force search or utilizing an approximate solution for MIVP. We conduct an experimental evaluation of our algorithm on various 2D grid layouts to assess its performance. We observe that our algorithm delivers outstanding results on small-sized and medium-sized layouts but struggles with larger layouts. We also contribute an interesting theoretical finding - the exact computation of MWIVD through a brute-force search is feasible but highly impractical due to its exponential time complexity.  We further analyze the problem's theoretical aspects by calculating the number of possible solutions for MWIVD on an n x n grid layout as 2^n^2 - n^2. We provide an upper bound for the ratio of the optimal solution to the total number of possible solutions as (n^2 - 1)/2^n^2. We also derive an lower bound for the average size of the optimal solution on an n x n grid layout as (n^2 - 1)/e. We conduct another experimental evaluation of the upper bound on various 2D grid layouts to assess its accuracy. We observe that the upper bound delivers outstanding results on small-sized and medium-sized layouts but struggles with larger layouts.  We conclude that the theoretical aspects of MWIVD offer valuable insights into the problem's behavior.  We also explore the computational complexity of MWIVD by calculating the number of possible solutions for MWIVD on an n x n grid layout as 2^(n^2) for an all-disjoint version of the problem. We contribute an interesting theoretical finding - the all-disjoint version of MWIVD is computationally intractable but can be solved through a brute-force search on a 3 x 3 grid layout.

With its high sensitivity and resolution, DALT could provide accurate measurements of D-alpha line emissions, enabling researchers to analyze the observatory's data and contribute to the system's scientific capabilities. Considering the system's proposed location and the DALT system's specifications, we evaluated the observatory's potential to detect and observe D-alpha line emissions in massive and late-type stars for various distances and stellar masses. Our results indicate that a DALT system with a 10-meter telescope could effectively observe massive stars with masses between 15 and 25 solar masses when they experience mass loss events, and could observe late-type stars with masses between 0.5 and 1.5 solar masses when they experience eruption events. We also examined the system's ability to detect emission peaks in massive stars and found that a 10-meter telescope might not be sufficient for observing stars with masses above 25 solar masses, although a larger telescope could make a difference. Once the inclination angle of the binary system is known, this method can accurately calculate the luminosity of the merger's gamma-ray signal. Since the inclination angle is difficult to determine precisely, binary system mergers with low mass ratios are more challenging to measure. The inclination angle of a gamma-ray siren's signal is directly tied to observing the binary system's neutron stars through radio telescopes at the time of the merger. It can also determine the inclination angle of a binary system merger quickly, allowing more precise measurements to be made through additional observing time. Despite its theoretical prediction over three decades ago, the GW memory has yet to be directly observed by gravitational wave detectors.  In order to search for the GW memory in binary neutron star mergers, we develop a novel method that incorporates the effects of the memory through the parameter estimation of gravitational wave observations. Based on our results, we conclude that third-generation gravitational wave detectors will be capable of detecting the GW memory in binary neutron star mergers within a few hundred megasecond mark, potentially enabling the detection of the GW memory through observational data.  Furthermore, we examine the prospects of detecting the GW memory through observational data through a combination of different gravitational wave detector configurations.  Finally, we explore the prospects of detecting the GW memory in binary black hole mergers with the next generation of gravitational wave detectors. We also contribute the effects of the memory to the analysis of existing gravitational wave events, which could lead to a reinterpretation of their astrophysical implications. Furthermore, we explored the phase transition's behavior in systems subject to a long-range interaction that is proportional to a particle's energy and analyzed the transition's conditions in systems driven by a harmonic oscillator model. The phase transition's boundary line was also found to correlate with the system's largest eigenvalue of the linearized Boltzmann operator. This problem can be seen as a variation of the classic discrete crystal base problem in combinatorics, specifically for the polynomial equation $x^n = 1$, which is well-understood. The solution approach we present mirrors that of the classic problem's solution. It involves calculating the number of lattice points for a general polynomial equation of degree $d$, then using that information to calculate the sum of squares of lattice points for a specific equation of the form $x^n - 1 = 0$, and finally applying the results to a product of distinct prime numbers to obtain the desired modulo $N$ value. The key components of this approach include applying the inclusion-exclusion principle, utilizing the concept of a root system, and applying the Euler product formula. The overall process results in an algorithm that calculates the desired value. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm using several examples.  The contribution of this research lies in its establishment of a solution strategy for the problem at hand, as well as its utilization of the inclusion-exclusion principle in a unique manner. It is also notable for its application of the Euler product formula in a discrete setting, which offers possibilities for future research.  The manuscript is structured to promote clarity, beginning with an introduction that sets the context and outlining the problem-solving approach before delving into the detailed calculation process. The research outcomes are presented in three parts, each focusing on a distinct polynomial equation scenario. The first scenario involves a single polynomial equation of degree $d$, the second involves a product of three polynomial equations of degree $3$, and the third involves a product of $r$ polynomial equations of degree $2$. The research concludes with an overview of the achieved results and their potential implications.  The manuscript includes three figures to illustrate the root system diagrams for the examples presented.  The author has included a proposal for future research at the end of the document. We present a novel perspective on solving these equations by leveraging the inverse scattering transformation, particularly for initial value problems, by reinterpreting the spectral data obtained from the discrete linear problem through a complex potential shift.  This shift enables the reconstruction of the initial condition from the spectral data, allowing for the solution of initial value problems for these equations, and it also leads to a straightforward computation of the initial condition's norm for the Korteweg--de Vries equation.  This approach differs from conventional methods that involve a space-time potential shift due to its computational efficiency and its suitability for initializing data with discontinuities.  This new approach shares similarities with the $L^p$-Bargmann invariant for Schr\"odinger equations; however, it stands in contrast to the $L^2$-Bargmann invariant due to its application to equations with a higher order nonlinearity.   limitations, primarily due to inaccuracies in representing complex chemical reactions
  and the high costs associated with simulating large biological systems. To address
  these issues, the development of machine-learning (ML) extensions to classical FFs,
  such as REUSABLE force fields (FFRs) like Generative Pre-trained Repressible Models
  (GPRMs), offers a promising solution. These FFRs resemble a "google map" of possible
  molecular conformations, allowing systems to sample chemical reactions and adapt
  to unique environments without the need for simulation. However, the high cost of
  pre-training these FFRs prohibits their widespread utilization, limiting their
  applicability to highly researched areas like prostaglandin synthesis.  A novel,
  pre-trained GPRM called "OMA" has recently been released, offering a viable option
  for biosynthetic pathways involving oxygen atoms.  To evaluate the effectiveness
  of this GPRM in biosynthetic pathways, it is being compared to the established
  SMIRNOV+ method for the synthesis of prostaglandins, a highly oxygenated molecule. 
  This comparison demonstrates that the GPRM outperforms the SMIRNOV+ method in generating
  prostaglandin structures, with more accurate oxygen atom placements and lower
  energy scores.  This GPRM can be utilized through an open-source software package
  called "Avogadro" to aid in the biosynthetic construction of oxygenated molecules. 
  This package includes a graphical user interface for configuring GPRM parameters,
  allowing users to tailor the model's behavior for specific biosynthetic scenarios. 
  This package also includes a scriptable interface for incorporating the GPRM into
  external workflows and a documentation that outlines the theoretical fundamentals
  of GPRMs.  This study aims to contribute to the development of effective ML-based
  FFs by providing a thorough analysis of GPRM performance in biosynthetic pathways. 
  This analysis offers valuable insights for the design of future GPRM architectures
  and the development of ML-based FFs suitable for various biosynthetic scenarios.

  molecules and offers a promising solution for improving biosynthetic constructions
  of natural products in chemistry simulations.

As a result, ensuring the proper functioning of these contracts is paramount, which is why we conducted a comprehensive, automated testing suite for Ethereum-based smart contracts, specifically for the Atomic Cross-Chain Swapping Protocol.  Our suite consisted of over 960 tests, which we ran on a test network, and it took around 35 minutes to complete.  We observed that our suite detected a critical bug in a previous implementation of the protocol, which we were able to fix by modifying the contract's logic.  We also measured the suite's effectiveness by simulating real-world scenarios, which included malicious actors and unexpected events, and it proved effective in verifying the behavior of the protocol in these situations.  We believe our testing suite serves as a model for other high-stakes smart contract protocols, and we contributed the suite's code to the public repository for use by others.  We also conducted an economic analysis of the costs associated with testing the suite, which consisted of around 960 tests that took 35 minutes to complete on a test network, and we observed that the gas costs amounted to around $120, which is equivalent to around $0.06 per test.  We propose a testing-as-a-service model for high-stakes smart contract protocols, where a pool of computers dedicated to testing these contracts could be funded through a small transaction fee on each contract deployment, and we estimate that this model could be viable for protocols with a large user base.  We also contribute a mathematical formula for calculating the optimal size of this pool based on various factors, which include the number of tests, the gas cost of each test, the total number of contract deployments per year, and the desired level of coverage.  We observe that the testing time for our suite could be significantly reduced by utilizing more powerful computers, but we note that faster computers do not necessarily result in more cost-effective testing, and we propose a plan to conduct further research on this topic.  We believe that our testing suite, along with our economic analysis and proposed testing-as-a-service model, contributes significantly to the development of reliable, trustworthy smart contract protocols.  We anticipate that our research will have a positive impact on the creation of high-stakes smart contract protocols and the improvement of existing ones.  We contribute our code to the public repository for use by others and we propose a plan to conduct further research on various aspects of automated testing for high-stakes smart contract protocols

Despite their success, the high computational cost of contrastive learning prevents its widespread adoption in real-world applications. Furthermore, existing studies on the computational efficiency of contrastive learning are limited to memory optimization and hardware acceleration, which fall short of addressing the fundamental issue with the algorithm's complexity. In contrast, this paper explores the theoretical foundations of contrastive learning, re-examining the need for comparing similar and dissimilar samples and analyzing the algorithm's objective function. Building on these analyses, we identify two major issues with the conventional contrastive loss function that contribute to its high computational requirement. To address these issues, we propose two modified contrastive learning frameworks -- one utilizing a simplified loss function and the other incorporating a regularization term -- along with corresponding algorithmic implementations. To evaluate these proposals, we conduct extensive experiments on few-shot learning tasks using real-world datasets, demonstrating their effectiveness over existing methods. Our research provides a theoretical basis for optimizing contrastive learning algorithms and offers practical guidelines for designing efficient contrastive learning strategies. method is widely used for simulating free surface flows, and its accuracy relies on the representation of the free surface interface.  Direct numerical simulations using VOF typically resolve the free surface interface, yet even with high resolution, the method may struggle with capturing sharp interfaces and can produce inaccuracies such as spurious curvature and detachment.  To address these issues, a new approach has been developed where the VOF method is coupled with a sharp interface capture technique, specifically a level set method, to simulate breaking waves in incompressible flow.  This new scheme reduces the free surface interface to a set of discrete points, eliminating the problems associated with spurious curvature and detachment, while also improving the simulation of wave breaking by enabling the creation of new free surfaces.  To evaluate the performance of this new approach, simulations of breaking waves were conducted and compared with experimental data, revealing that the method could generate realistic profiles of breaking waves for moderate wind speeds.  However, it failed to simulate the formation of crests in extremely strong winds likely due to the limitations of the model in representing highly curved free surface interfaces.  Additionally, the approach demonstrated better performance over a similar scheme using a ghost fluid method, likely due to the more accurate representation of normal velocities at the free surface interface.  To further assess the validity of the new approach, simulations of wave impact loads on a structure were carried out and compared with impact loads measured during experiments, showing that the simulation could accurately predict the impact duration and load for a structure exposed to a single breaking wave but overestimated the load for multiple breaking waves likely due to the limitations of the model in representing multiple breaking waves.  Finally, the study demonstrated the effectiveness of the new approach in simulating breaking waves for the purpose of analyzing wave impact loads on structures, highlighting its potential applications in the design of coastal and offshore structures.  The new VOF-level set method was also found to be computationally efficient, taking significantly less time to simulate a breaking wave under moderate wind conditions using 100000 grid points than using 1500000 grid points with the standard VOF method, demonstrating its capability to reduce simulation costs without compromising accuracy.  The study provides a comprehensive framework for using the VOF-level set method in simulating breaking waves and other free surface flows with sharp interfaces, offering a viable option for industrial applications.  The paper concludes by outlining several areas for future research, including the development of a more robust sharp interface capture technique and the implementation of the method in more complex flow models. While fractures filled with magma can provide significant conductivity, fractures empty of magma may act as barriers to conductivity.  Understanding the dynamics of fractures is crucial for determining how mantle reservoirs generate and sustain permeability that fuels lava flows.  A previous study found that fractures within deeply layered mantle reservoirs that produce long-lived lava flows tend to be oriented vertically, whereas those producing short-lived flows are more horizontally aligned.  This research explores the effective stress theory to understand how fractures respond to pressure and fluid pressure variations that influence their connectivity and overall permeability of the reservoir.  Fractures filled with a fluid, such as magma, experience a decrease in effective stress compared to dry fractures, making them more prone to sliding and opening when subjected to shear stress.  On the other hand, empty fractures behave like dry fractures and may close under increasing effective stress.  A model simulating the growth of fractures under effective stress conditions found that fractures inclined at a low angle within deeply layered reservoirs produce more abundant edge connections when filled with a fluid, contributing to higher conductivity values.  Fractures inclined at a high angle produce fewer edge connections when empty, leading to lower conductivity values. Although there are numerous algorithms for achieving DP when publishing a single dataset, many challenges arise when publishing combined data sets from multiple parties due to the difficulty in verifying the integrity of other parties' data.  An adversary could potentially manipulate their data in a way that affects the privacy of another party's data, compromising the DP guarantee.  This paper addresses this problem by introducing a new concept of privacy called "relative" DP, which provides an accurate measure of how much an adversary can learn about each party's data by observing the combined data set. The first protocol ensures relative DP when publishing combined data sets from multiple parties, with each party publishing their data separately.  The second protocol can be used when one party possesses multiple data sets, with the option of publishing combined or individual data sets in various ways.  Both protocols offer improved relative DP guarantees over previous approaches, demonstrating an exponential improvement in scenarios with multiple parties and/or multiple data sets. We investigate the optimal time to implement and lift social distancing measures within a mathematical compartment-based model that accounts for both the economic costs of restrictions and the benefits of preventing virus transmissions. Our results show that the strategy that minimizes the combination of infection cases and economic loss is to implement measures when a significant number of cases have occurred and lift them once the infection peak has passed. A novel observation that validation set verification methods often fail for certain problematic inputs has led to a re-examination of their purpose.  In fact, it was found that these methods consistently output high confidence errors when applying models to data from adversarial attack creation processes, despite these processes aiming to mislead models.  This unexpected behavior suggests that validation set verification methods function similarly to output verification methods, which was previously a controversial idea.  This similarity in function has significant implications, as it implies that both techniques measure the model's reliability based on the margin of output labels.  This understanding can lead to the development of more effective output verification methods, which is demonstrated by a novel algorithm presented in the paper.  This algorithm, called "Boundary Regularized Training", has been proven theoretically to improve the reliability of neural networks in sensitive regions of the input space and has been verified through experimental results.  This research contributes to our knowledge of neural network reliability and has practical applications in developing and deploying robust neural network models.  Code for the research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/chenzhou128/BRT.  The paper's findings advocate for treating validation set verification methods as output verification methods when assessing the reliability of neural networks.  This recognition can help avoid overestimating a model's performance and encourage the development of more robust models that function accurately even when applying outputs to tight boundaries of the input space. Although previous research suggested that binary S-boxes based on permutation tables are highly vulnerable to PSCA,  it does not account for S-boxes utilized in Simon and Simeon blockchain cryptocurrencies.  Furthermore, it assumes the attack requires significant data that is not feasible in real-world scenarios.  On the other hand, binary S-boxes based on permutation matrices are considered secure against PSCA.  However, our research found that S-boxes used in Simeon are susceptible to PSCA when employing the Hill climbing algorithm and when the attack uses moderate data.  On the other hand, S-boxes employed in Simon are resistant to PSCA.  We also observed that PSCA is effective against S-boxes based on permutation tables but requires a more efficient search algorithm.  Our findings are significant as they provide an accurate assessment of the vulnerability of block ciphers to PSCA prior to its anticipated real-world application.  Furthermore, our research lays the groundwork for conducting PSCA on real-world block ciphers used in blockchain cryptocurrencies.  Moreover, it offers block cipher designers with valuable information on how to fortify their block ciphers against PSCA.  We believe that our research will have a positive impact on improving the security of block ciphers and blockchain cryptocurrencies.  Finally, our research contributes substantially to the block cipher security database by discovering new permutation attacks on various block ciphers.  Specifically, we discovered that Tiax-64, ARIA-128, Camellia-256, GOSTR-128, and GOSTR-256 are susceptible to PSCA.  We also found that the scope of PSCA extends to stream ciphers, discovering an attack on the HC-256 stream cipher used in Simeon.  Our research demonstrates that PSCA offers a valuable side-channel analysis method for evaluating block and stream ciphers.  We propose several proposals to mitigate PSCA, recommending the use of countermeasures such as masking, dual-rail precharge logic, and transient power countermeasures.  We also suggest that block ciphers with low data complexity are vulnerable to PSCA and advocate for conducting side-channel attack tests on real-world block ciphers used in blockchain cryptocurrencies.  We believe that our research will have a positive impact on improving the security of block ciphers and blockchain cryptocurrencies.
